explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says Miriam and Aaron criticized Moses “…because of the Cushite woman he had married, for he had taken a Cushite wife.” That's the reason the passage gives, so I'll leave it right there. Two siblings, one complaint, and the LORD heard it (Numbers 12:2). That's a lot of weight for one complaint to carry.

The seventy elders do show up earlier in Numbers. The LORD told Moses to gather seventy of Israel's elders (Numbers 11:16). But that's not what Miriam and Aaron are fussing about here. The text says it's about the Cushite woman Moses married.

explanations.answer: The way he led them out
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd guess it, friend. Leaders get complaints about everything. But the passage doesn't say a word about that. It says they criticized Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married.

You've got it. They ask, “Does the LORD speak only through Moses?” and then, “Does He not also speak through us?” They're pointing at themselves. That's the whole point of the questions, and the LORD hears every word.

explanations.answer: He has stopped speaking at all
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not the point, friend. Miriam and Aaron aren't saying the LORD has gone quiet. They ask, “Does He not also speak through us?” That's about Him speaking through them as well.

explanations.answer: He only speaks through the elders
explanations.explanation: The elders don't come up in their questions at all, baker. Miriam and Aaron ask whether the LORD speaks only through Moses, and then whether He also speaks through them. They're making a point about themselves, not the elders.

I wish it worked that way, friend. You know when you say something you figure nobody will ever hear, and then you find out it got around? Here, the text says plainly, “And the LORD heard this.” So it didn't stay between the two of them.
Right, baker. After Miriam and Aaron ask their questions, the text says, “And the LORD heard this.” That's the moment everything turns. Their conversation was not private after all.
That's it, friend. The LORD says to Moses, Aaron and Miriam, “You three, come out to the Tent of Meeting.” The text says He spoke suddenly. I think I'd have dropped my whole tray of cookies.
Mount Sinai is a famous spot, so I see why it came to mind. But this passage doesn't send anyone up a mountain. The LORD tells the three to come out to the Tent of Meeting.
The Jordan isn't mentioned in this passage, baker. The LORD's words are, “You three, come out to the Tent of Meeting.” That's where the three go, and it's where He comes down to meet them.

Yes, baker. The LORD came down in a pillar of cloud, stood at the entrance to the Tent, and summoned Aaron and Miriam. The two who did the talking are the two who get called forward. Moses isn't in that pair.

Close, friend, but Miriam is the one in the pair. The text says the LORD summoned Aaron and Miriam, and both of them stepped forward. Moses was one of the three who went out, but he isn't the one called up.
Half right, baker, because Miriam is in. But Aaron is the other one. The LORD summoned Aaron and Miriam, and both of them stepped forward.

True, friend. The LORD says, “But this is not so with My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house.” He calls Moses His servant and says it right in front of Aaron and Miriam. That's a strong thing to hear the LORD say about you.
He does say it, baker. The LORD tells Aaron and Miriam, “But this is not so with My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house.” That's how He describes Moses to them.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “I speak with him face to face, clearly and not in riddles…” That's how plainly He speaks with Moses. With me, a recipe that says 'bake until done' is about as clear as a riddle.
That word isn't in the verse, friend. The LORD says He speaks with Moses face to face, “…clearly and not in riddles…” He says nothing there about how often. The point is how plain the speaking is.
Nothing in the verse about how long, baker. The LORD says He speaks with Moses “…face to face, clearly and not in riddles…” The word that fits is clearly.

True, friend. The text says, “So the anger of the LORD burned against them, and He departed.” This is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't soften it. After the question He asked, the anger is what comes next.
It's the other way, baker. The text says, “So the anger of the LORD burned against them, and He departed.” That's a heavy line, and the passage lets it stand. The anger burns, and then He leaves.

Yes, friend. Aaron turns, sees Miriam, and says to Moses, “My lord, please do not hold against us this sin we have so foolishly committed.” He's speaking to the very one he and Miriam spoke against. That's a humbling moment.

Joshua is Moses' assistant (Numbers 11:28), so I get why he came to mind, friend. But the passage doesn't mention him in this scene. Aaron turns and speaks to Moses: “My lord, please do not hold against us this sin we have so foolishly committed.” The name that fits here is Moses.

Caleb, from the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6), isn't named in this scene, baker. Nobody else steps in here. Aaron's words go straight to Moses: “My lord, please do not hold against us this sin we have so foolishly committed.” So Moses is the answer.

explanations.answer: Not to hold their sin against them
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Aaron says, “My lord, please do not hold against us this sin we have so foolishly committed.” He says 'us,' not just 'her.' He calls it a sin and a foolish one, and I think that's a hard thing to say out loud.

explanations.answer: To send Miriam far from the camp
explanations.explanation: Aaron asks for the opposite kind of thing, friend. He pleads with Moses not to hold their sin against them. Being confined outside the camp comes later, and it's the LORD who says it, in His answer to Moses.

explanations.answer: To let the elders judge the matter
explanations.explanation: The elders never come up in Aaron's words, baker. He says, “My lord, please do not hold against us this sin we have so foolishly committed.” His plea is aimed straight at Moses.

explanations.answer: Cries out to God to heal her
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. Moses cried out to the LORD, “O God, please heal her!” The one Miriam and Aaron criticized is the one who pleads for Miriam. I think that says a lot about Moses, and the text has just called him “…a very humble man…” (Numbers 12:3).

explanations.answer: Tells Aaron to pray for her instead
explanations.explanation: That's not what Moses does, baker. He doesn't hand it off to anyone. He cries out to the LORD himself, “O God, please heal her!”

explanations.answer: Asks the elders to decide for him
explanations.explanation: No elders in this moment, friend. The text says Moses cried out to the LORD, “O God, please heal her!” He takes it straight to God.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, “Let her be confined outside the camp for seven days…” The text gives it as a set number. I can't even keep a batch in the oven for a set number without checking it six times.

Forty is a fair guess, friend. Forty shows up in big moments, like the forty days and forty nights of rain in Genesis 7:12. But here the LORD says, “Let her be confined outside the camp for seven days…” Seven is the number in this verse, and after that she may be brought back in.
A month is a lot longer than what the text says, friend. The LORD says, “Let her be confined outside the camp for seven days…” That's one week, and then she may be brought back in.
True, baker. The LORD says, “after that she may be brought back in.” The seven days come with an ending. That's good news.
Good news hides in that one, friend. The LORD says, “Let her be confined outside the camp for seven days; after that she may be brought back in.” So the confinement has an end, and she comes back in.
Yes, friend. The text says, “…the people did not move on until she was brought in again.” The whole camp waits for Miriam. They stay where they are until she's back.
It's the opposite, baker. The text says, “…the people did not move on until she was brought in again.” They stay where they are for all seven days.
Nothing in the text about the people splitting up, friend. It says, “…the people did not move on until she was brought in again.” They stay put as one camp until she's back.
